text.p: In overnight commodity markets, copper prices rose on the London Metal Exchange in expectation of another drop in copper stocks.
Gold prices also ended firmer in New York, but only slightly, ahead of the U.S. presidential elections and economic data.
Oil prices fell after the market discounted news that a U.S. jet fighter fired at an Iraqi position over the weekend.
Wheat prices rose on news of Pakistani purchases of U.S. wheat.

Copper prices rose on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Monday, buoyed by expectations of another drop in stocks on Tuesday, traders and analysts said. But all base metal markets finished the day below the highs as softening nearby spreads on copper undermined the complex.
"Copper looked set to have a look at $2,000 (a tonne), but the easing spread was the main inhibitive factor," said Robin Bhar, analyst at LME ring dealers Brandeis.
Three month copper futures finished the afternoon kerb at $1,972 a tonne, up $14 from Friday's close but well below the day's high of $1,985.
LME stocks are at six-year lows of 123,700 tonnes and are forecast to fall another 5,000 to 10,000 tonnes on Tuesday.
Other base metals finished lower in mostly routine trade, although tin dipped briefly to a 17-month nadir of $5,890 before recovering slightly. Zinc lost ground, slipping to $1,066 from $1,073.50.
Nickel fell slightly to $7,160 from $7,190. Aluminium held steady despite copper's weakness, ending just $0.50 softer at $1,424.50.

COMEX copper ended a dull session barely firmer as the market remained steady ahead of Tuesday's LME stock report. December COMEX settled 0.80 cent firmer at 93.45 cents, trading 93.70 to 92.00 cents.

New York precious metals futures ended slightly higher Monday, with the complex again failing to follow through to the downside, but volumes were very light, traders said. "Gold is continuing to erode away in a very slow but steady fashion with most bullion dealers looking for $375 basis spot as their first downside target in coming weeks," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said. COMEX December gold ended up 40 cents at $379.60 an ounce, after seeing life-of-contract low last week at $377.70. In the bullion market, gold ended quoted $378.60/379.00 an ounce, compared to the London Monday afternoon fix at $378.70 and the New York close Friday at $378.00/378.50. Spot gold saw its lowest levels since March 1995 last week at $376.70.

NYMEX crude and heating oil futures fell on Monday in a continuation of the sell-off which began two weeks ago on diminishing worries about low inventories. Gasoline futures rose modestly as recent refinery problems in the Gulf of Mexico and a switch away from gasoline production helped reverse gasoline's previous seasonal price decline. Dec crude closed 28 cents lower at $22.75 a barrel, while Dec heating oil was off 0.80 cents at 65.80 cents a gallon. "Everything was real quiet most of the day

with very low volumes. The outlook is still sideways, lower; it's still in trouble," said a NYMEX trader at brokerage Prudential. The market quickly discounted news over the weekend that a U.S. jet fighter fired at an Iraqi position, the Prudential trader said. And there wasn't much reaction to news that Sun Co would keep an 80,000 crude distillation unit at its Marcus Hook refinery down an extra month after a scheduled maintenance because of poor margins, he added.

CBOT wheat futures were higher at the midsession on a technical correction tied to signals the market was oversold for the near term, traders said. News that Pakistan bought 270,000 tonnes of U.S. soft white wheat and that Turkey may relax U.S. wheat import restrictions may have buoyed the market. At 1204 CST, wheat was two to six cents per bushel higher, with December up 5-3/4 at $3.80-1/2. Wheat prices were kept on the defensive by news the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) cut wheat prices and increased to 21 million tonnes its estimate of Australia's wheat production. The AWB's previous estimate was 20 million tonnes.
